items.topic: Option payoffs are asymmetric, which links option value to volatility
items.definition: Because an option's payout is asymmetric (the buyer's downside is capped while upside is not), the buyer and seller of an option are affected differently by volatility.
items.core_idea: A large price move, even one with equal odds of going up or down, benefits an option buyer more than it benefits the seller, since the buyer's losses are capped but gains are not — so buyers want volatility and sellers want price stability.
key_points: Option payoffs are asymmetric: the buyer's potential loss is limited (to the premium paid), but potential profit is not
A 50/50 chance of a big move still favors the option buyer over the seller because of this asymmetry
Option buyers benefit from large price moves in either direction; option sellers benefit when prices stay stable
relationships: Underpins why volatility is priced into options, connecting to the Greeks (esp. Vega) discussed next
trading_implications: Sellers of options need to be compensated through premium for taking on volatility exposure
Volatility itself becomes a distinct, tradable risk factor separate from price direction

source.section_hint: Options and Volatility (lead-in to Deltas, Gammas, and Other Greeks)

items.topic: The Greeks: standardized option sensitivity measures
items.definition: The Greeks are a standard set of sensitivity measures, each named after a Greek letter, that quantify how an option's (or asset's) value responds to a change in one specific underlying factor.
items.core_idea: Sensitivity analysis lets a trader isolate how much P&L would result from a specific kind of change — in price, volatility, time, or interest rates — so risk can be decomposed factor by factor instead of only viewed as a single aggregate exposure.
key_points: A Greek is never a standalone number like a price — it is always a comparison of how one asset's value responds to changes in an underlying
Delta: the P&L that results when the underlying's price changes
Gamma: the change in Delta itself when the underlying's price changes
Vega: the P&L that results when the underlying's volatility changes
Theta: the P&L that results from the passage of time (commonly measured per day)
Rho: the P&L that results when the interest rate changes
relationships: Vega formalizes the volatility sensitivity described in the option/volatility discussion just before this section
trading_implications: Traders use the Greeks to answer targeted 'what happens if X moves' questions about a position without repricing the whole book
Because Greeks isolate individual risk factors, they let a portfolio's exposure be managed factor-by-factor (e.g., hedging Delta separately from Vega)

items.topic: Spread options and why they dominate energy derivatives
items.definition: A spread option is an option whose payoff depends on the difference between two asset prices exceeding a strike level, rather than a single asset price exceeding a strike — equivalent to a normal option with a variable strike price.
items.core_idea: Spread options are especially common in energy markets because so much of energy trading and physical operations is really about capturing the spread between two prices (location, time, or input/output) relative to the cost of bridging that spread, and because correlation between the two underlying prices — not just their individual volatilities — dominates how these options are valued.
key_points: Can be structured as an option directly on the spread (spread treated as the 'price'), or by folding the second asset's price into an effective strike

Prevalent in energy because deals commonly hinge on: price here vs. price there vs. transportation cost (location), price now vs. price later vs. storage cost (time), and fuel price vs. power price vs. conversion cost (input/output)
Valuing a spread option is materially harder than valuing a single-asset option because the correlation between the two underlying assets becomes the single most important valuation input
Correlation between two highly correlated assets produces very different spread behavior than correlation between uncorrelated assets
Correlation is difficult to estimate: historical data can be misleading, and there usually isn't a liquid enough market to infer what correlation other market participants are using
Correlation risk must be actively monitored for the entire life of the trade, not just estimated once at trade inception

trading_implications: Firms trading spread options need infrastructure specifically for monitoring correlation risk between products
Misestimating correlation is called out as the single easiest way to mis-value an option position
common_misunderstandings: Assuming a spread option can be valued like two independent single-asset options, when correlation between the two legs is actually the dominant valuation driver

items.topic: Electricity price formation via merit-order auctions
items.definition: ISOs set electricity prices through non-discriminatory auctions: power plants submit bids, the ISO dispatches the lowest bidders first, and every dispatched plant is paid the same clearing price — the price bid by the marginal (last-needed) plant.
items.core_idea: Because all winning generators receive the same uniform clearing price regardless of their own bid, the plants that sit at the margin — the last one turned on or the next one that would be turned off — are disproportionately influential in setting the market price.
key_points: Power plants submit quotes/bids to the ISO to be selected for operation
Plants are dispatched from lowest bid to highest bid until demand is met; plants are continually activated and deactivated as demand changes
Every operating plant is paid the same price: the price set by the marginal plant (the last one activated, or the next one that would be deactivated)
Most power markets run two auctions: a day-ahead auction the day before delivery, plus real-time auctions to cover unexpected shortfalls
Marginal plants — those right at the activation/deactivation threshold — are the most influential in setting the market-clearing price
relationships: Sets up the more detailed 'generation stack' discussion of bidding strategy that follows
trading_implications: Traders track which plants are near the margin, since their bidding behavior drives the clearing price
Understanding the bid stack (merit order) helps anticipate when and how prices will move
common_misunderstandings: Assuming generators are paid their own bid price (pay-as-bid) rather than the uniform marginal clearing price

items.topic: Spatial load forecasting, base load, and peak demand
items.definition: Spatial load forecasting predicts where and when electricity demand ('load') will occur; because electricity cannot be stored, supply must be generated to match forecasted demand in real time.
items.core_idea: Grid operators rely on short-term load forecasts to schedule generation and maintenance and on long-term forecasts to plan infrastructure, with two key demand benchmarks — base load (the always-on minimum) and peak demand (the maximum) — anchoring both operational and trading decisions.
key_points: 'Load' is used synonymously with electricity demand throughout this discussion
Most regions have a relatively constant baseline demand; most short-term variability in demand comes from weather
Over long time frames (e.g., a decade), economic growth and residential trends also become significant demand drivers
Short-term load forecasts are used to schedule power plant operation and maintenance
Long-term load forecasts are used to plan new transmission lines, new power plants, and other infrastructure
Base load power is the minimum amount of power that must be supplied to the grid at any time; it sets a floor on how many plants must run continuously year-round
Peak demand is the maximum amount of power expected to be required at any time
Grid operators use peak demand estimates for capacity planning; traders use the same estimates to anticipate how often and when price spikes will occur
relationships: Feeds directly into the merit-order/generation stack pricing mechanic — demand forecasts determine how far up the bid stack the ISO must dispatch
trading_implications: Peak demand forecasts help traders anticipate the frequency and timing of price spikes
